all saint. ‘the ultimate object of veneration of the saints is the glory of god and the sanctification of man by conforming one’s life fully to the divine will and by imitating the virtue of those who were pre-eminent disciples of the lord. catechises and other forms of doctrinal instruction should therefore make known to the faithful that our relationship with the saints must be seen in the light of the faith and should not obscure the “cultus latriae due to god the father through christ in the holy spirit, but intensify it ” november – why bother having a funeral mass? why not just go straight to the cemetery and leave out the funeral mass? in times gone by every catholic who died automatically came to the church for their funeral. in the recent times some families bypass the church and do not bring their dead to the church for the requiem or funeral mass. instead they go straight to the cemetery or crematorium. in doing so they leave jesus out. they forget that we are not merely individuals, we are part of a community of friends of jesus called the church. it is sad to see people who loved the mass and came to mass regularly not being brought to the church and giving their friends and fellow christians in the parish a chance to mark their passing with the greatest gift god has given us, the mass. why is it important to have a funeral mass? every catholic is baptized into god’s holy trinity, uniting themselves with jesus and his church. we are baptized into the death and resurrection of jesus from the dead because jesus has conquered death and opened for us the way to eternal life. so it does not make sense to leave jesus out of the equation. jesus is the whole reason for baptism, and especially for the mass. we expect to meet jesus when we die. the funeral mass is the heart of our funeral – jesus gave us the mass at the last supper just before he died on the cross. the mass only makes sense because jesus conquered death and evil by rising from the dead on easter sunday. remember the acclamation at the solemn consecration of the mass “christ has died, christ is risen, christ will come again ”. in the funeral mass we offer our dead to the father as jesus did for us on the cross. the funeral mass asks god to admit the dead catholic to the paschal fullness of the table of the kingdom. through baptism we become part of god’s family – the parish community. it is by the mass and holy communion that the community of the faithful, especially the family of the deceased, learn to live in communion with the one who "has fallen asleep in the lord," by communicating in the body of christ of which he is a living member and, then, by praying for him and with him. for christians to forget about the church funeral for the dead is to leave out the main player, jesus christ, who is our saviour. the greatest act of love you can do for your loved one who dies is to give them the gift of a catholic funeral with the complete rites of the church in accord with god’s wish for each and every member of his church when they die. saturday 31st october 6.30pm tom & rosaleen feely (anniv) grainne long (anniv) sunday 1st november 11.30am mary our beloved dead, who continue to pray for us .” in november, we specially remember the faithful departed who have gone before us to god. it is often called the month of the holy souls when we recall people we knew in this life and also those who may have no one to pray for them. many people choose to commemorate their deceased family and friends by adding their names to the parish altar list of the dead. it’s an important tradition to maintain every year as those whose names are on the altar list of the dead are remembered regularly at masses throughout the year. our gospel today is the beatitudes which can be described as a charter for christian living which perfectly describe her life. reading it today, it appears to be counter cultural as it turns many of today’s values on their head. they go to the very centre of our lives as christians and invite us to follow a way of life that may not come naturally to us. however, the very words that jesus uses here “gentle”, “merciful”, “pure in heart”, “peacemaker” are an appropriate description of kay’s g ood and generous life. jesus also challenges us by referring to those who hunger and thirst for what is right”. pope benedict tried to explain the meaning of life after death within the limitations of our language and understanding. i hope that their reflections below will offer some consolation especially to those amongst us who may have lost a friend or family member in the past year and are particularly feeling their absence around now. when speaking about the next life in 2012, pope benedict xvi sa id: “death opens to life, to eternal life, which is not an infinite duplicate of the present time, but something completely new.” in a beautiful reflection, pope benedict goes on to explain that: “our hope, then, lies in the love of god that shines resp lendent from the cross of christ who lets jesus’ words to the good thief: “today you will be with me in paradise” (lk 23:43) resound in our heart.” saint john henry newman in his poem “the dream of gerontius” describes the soul, approaching heaven, as it sees something of the divine vision: “a grand mysterious harmony: it floods me, like the deep and solemn sound of many waters.” pope john xxiii, now a saint, was once asked if he prayed for the dead. he replied: “i often think of the departed, they keep me good company.” there is an unbroken chain of connection with our beloved dead, who continue to pray for us in the presence of god, and ourselves as we continue to pray for them. we can be especially close to them during when we celebrate mass when our deceased relatives and friends are always remembered in the eucharistic prayer. may they rest in peace. amen. let us continue to pray for and remember our faithful departed during the month of november and be assured that they are praying for us as well. may we reflect on the lives of people who have inspired and helped us and are now enjoying the rewards of their goodness with the risen on this beautiful feast of all saints, we give thanks to god for the countless men and women who have faithfully followed christ and now share in the glory of heaven. some are well-known saints whom the church honours publicly; many others are ordinary people whose holiness was lived quietly in daily acts of faith, hope, and love. the saints remind us that holiness is not reserved for a select few. through baptism, each of us is called to become a saint and to reflect god's love in our families, workplaces, schools, and communitics. their lives encourage us to persevere in prayer, trust in god's mercy, and remain faithful in times of joy and difficulty. as we celebrate this feast, let us thank god for the saints who inspire us and remember with gratitude those holy people who have influenced our lives and helped us grow in faith. may their example guide us on our own journey towards the fullness of life with god. altar list of the dead: the altar list of the dead is ready at to be saints. we can try to do this by following the message and example of jesus, as shown in the gospel. jesus teaches the disciples god’s law in a new way, summed up in the beatitudes, are a map with of eight different paths. by following them, we align our lives with the heart of god and ‘holiness’. the first reading gives us a vision of heaven. those who belong to the lord are marked with a seal and kept safe, ‘an innumerable number from every nation, from all tribes and peoples. in the second reading, john addresses us as ‘beloved’, reminding us that we are children of god. although today’s world may misunderstand god’s way, we are promised eternal life when we will see god as he is. the psalmist sings of the created world and all dwelling in it. those who seek the lord’s face with clean hands and a pure heart will receive his blessing. on this feast, let’s pray for all those persecuted for their faith; of november 1st for the commemoration of all saints .[11]all saints' day is a solemnity in catholicism in the western christian practice, the liturgical celebration begins with its first vespers on the evening of october 31, all hallows' eve(all saints' eve or hallowe'en), and ends at the compline of november 1. it is thus the day before all souls' day , which commemorates the faithful departed. in many traditions, all saints' day is part of the season of allhallowtide , which includes the three days from october 31 to november 3 inclusive, in places where all saints' day is observed as a public holiday, cemetery and grave rituals such as offerings of flowers, candles and prayers or blessings for the graves of loved ones often take place on all saints' day (along with other days of allsaintstide, especially on all hallows eve and all souls day).[18][19][20][21][22] the ceremonial use of candles symbolize the light of christ and the use of lamps at the tombs of martyrs dates back he responded, “there were three old ladies, the janitor, several thousand archangels, a large number of seraphim, and several million of the triumphant saints of god”. but we always have room for one more! we should always keep in mind the great cloud of witnesses that surround us at every mass. so, on this feast we remember the many good people gone before us whom we’ve met in life and without embarrassment pray to them to help us on our journey . may we join them one day in the communion of saints. registration for children wishing to receive the sacraments of first communion or confirmation in our parish next year 2027 is open on our parish website. register using the link

. norms for indulgences at the commemoration of all souls 1. from 12 o’clock noon on 1st november until midnight on 2nd november, all who have confessed, received holy communion and prayed for the pope’s intentions (one our father and hail mary, or any other prayer of one’s choice) can gain one plenary indulgence by visiting a church or oratory, and there reciting one our father and the apostles’ creed. this indulgence is applicable only to the souls of the departed. confession may be made at any time within the week preceding or the week following 1st november. holy communion may be received on any day from 1st november to 8th november. 2. the faithful who visit a cemetery and pray for the dead may gain a plenary indulgence applicable only to the holy souls on the usual conditions once per day from 1st to 8th november. the conditions mentioned above apply also for this. norms for indulgences at the commemoration of all souls 1. from 12 o’clock noon on 1st november until midnight on 2nd november, all who have confessed, received holy communion and prayed for the pope’s intentions (one our father and hail mary, or any other prayer of one’s choice) can gain one plenary indulgence by visiting a church or oratory, and there reciting one our father and the apostles’ creed. this indulgence is applicable only to the souls of the departed. confession may be made at any time within the week preceding or the week following 1st november. holy communion may be received on any day from 1st november to 8th november. 2. the faithful who visit a cemetery and pray for the dead may gain a plenary indulgence applicable only to the holy souls on the usual conditions once per day from 1st to 8th november. the conditions mentioned above apply also for this. children’s corner; what do you remember from this weeks gospel? chapel of the blessed margaret ball, santry wed sun 10am think of the love that the father has lavished on us, by letting us be called god’s children; and that is what we are. because the world refused to acknowledge him, therefore it does not acknowledge us. my dear people, we are already the children of god but what we are to be in the future has not yet been revealed; all we know is, that when it is revealed we shall be like him because we shall see him as he really is. surely everyone who entertains this hope must purify himself, must try to be as pure as christ. second reading 1 john 3:1-3 we shall be like god because we shall see him as he really is gospel acclamation alleluia, alleluia! come to me, all you who labour and are overburdened and i will give you rest, says the lord. alleluia! matthew 5:1-12a seeing the crowds, jesus went up the hill. there he sat down and was joined by his disciples. then he began to speak. this is what he taught them: gospel how happy are the poor in spirit apocalypse 7:2-4, 9-14 first reading i saw a huge number, impossible to count, of people from every nation, race, tribe and language as we adore you, o god, who alone are holy and wonderful in all your saints, we implore your grace, so that, coming to perfect holiness in the fullness of your love, we may pass from this pilgrim table to the banquet of our heavenly homeland. through christ our lord. amen prayer after communion how happy are the poor in spirit; theirs is the kingdom of heaven. happy the gentle: they shall have the earth for their heritage. happy those who mourn: they shall be comforted. happy those who hunger and thirst for what is right: they shall be satisfied. happy the merciful: they shall have mercy shown them. happy the pure in heart: they shall see god. happy the peacemakers: they shall be called sons of god. happy those who are persecuted in the cause of right: theirs is the kingdom of heaven. ‘happy are you when people abuse you and persecute you and speak all kinds of calumny against you on my account. rejoice and be glad, for your reward will be great in heaven.’ the word of the lord readings for the solemnity of all saints 08:45 - 12:00 18:30 - 20:00 10:00 - 13:30 09.30 - 13:00 09:30 - 19:00 09:30 - 16:00

dates for your diary “holiness is not the luxury of the few; it is a simple duty for you and me.”st teresa of calcutta thought for the week the saints were ordinary people who let christ’s love conquer their weakness. which beatitude is jesus inviting me to live out more fully this week? to ponder this week men and women of the beatitudes hymns 10.30am mass, church of the holy child, whitehall opening hymn no.66, offertory hymn no.16 holy child nativity parishes beaumont | larkhill | whitehall | santry we lift our eyes to heaven to honour not only the known, canonised saints, but also the anonymous, quiet saints: the mothers and fathers who built society through daily devotion to their families, the priests and religious who were consumed like candles in service, and the missionaries who left everything to bring christ to the ends of the earth. this feast reminds us that holiness is a universal vocation—a beautiful, personal path that every baptised christian is uniquely capable of walking. the liturgy leads us up the mount of the beatitudes in the gospel of saint matthew, where jesus reveals the definitive blueprint for this journey. the beatitudes are the "magna charta" of the christian life. they turn worldly logic on its head, showing us that true happiness is found in meekness, purity of heart, mercy, and peacemaking. the saints are simply ordinary people who allowed themselves to become "men and women of the beatitudes," allowing christ's love to conquer human weakness. his sunday, we celebrate the solemnity of all saints, joining our hearts to the vast, uncountable multitude praised in the first reading from the apocalypse. in the light of the church's timeless teaching on this great feast, we are reminded that all saints' day is not just a commemoration of historical figures, but a vibrant thanksgiving for the wonders god has accomplished in human history through ordinary lives. year a | solemnity of all saints

pastors desk today, november 1st, the feast of all saints is a distinctive day in our catholic list of feast days. the church has a very precise process, called canonisation through which it feels confident to say that somebody has lived a life in tune with the will of god and has now reached the kingdom of heaven. however the church knows too that we can’t limit the number of people who have reached eternal happiness in continuation of their holy christian lives. they are people known to us – family, friends, colleagues and people like ourselves who have helped the thirsty, the hungry, those without clothes and shelter. the love of neighbour that, after our death leads to god’s right hand. these were the gestures that carried weight with jesus. the feast of all saints is a day of great hope and inspiration for us. as the epistle to the hebrews states “since we are surrounded by so great a cloud of witnesses, let us rid ourselves of every burden and sin that clings to us and persevere in running that lies before us.”(heb. 12:1) mass attendance a holy elderly priest was once asked, “how many people attended the early morning mass today”? he responded “ there were three old ladies, the janitor, several thousand archangels, a large number of seraphim, and several million of the triumphant saints of god”. but we always have room for one more! we should always keep in mind the great cloud of witnesses that surround us at every mass. so on this feast we remember the many good people gone before us whom we’ve met in life and without embarrassment pray to them to help us on our journey. may we join them one day in the communion of saints. st. paul’s parish ayrfield all saints day - a 1st november 2026

as promised, we publish this weekend the results of the recent mass count taken at the request of the archdiocese. there was no substantial change from previous years. our numbers continue to fluctuate depending on many factors, the weather, the amount of people coming to remember loved ones for anniversaries, months minds, timing, and other variants. it is thus difficult enough to get a real appraisal of how many are coming to mass on a regular basis. the highest number present for an individual mass was 342, the lowest 94. the average mass goers over the three weekends totalled 693. our church holds 1,500 people. we are also conscious of our online community. many parishes in the diocese have reduced their number of masses in the last number of years. as mentioned before it is getting harder to get mass cover when a priest is ill or away. we also have to keep in mind that the traditional individual parish is a thing of the past-we are all part of ‘partnerships of parishes’ and more is being asked of an aging priesthood. what we need to think about is not only the amount of masses, but the quality of the liturgies that are celebrated? do we need four weekend masses taking into account the above numbers? are the times of the masses suitable? should we have an earlier vigil mass especially in the darker winter months? i welcome your counsel and suggestions. fr michael masses 10 am monday to saturday, vigil mass saturday 6.30 pm sunday masses 9 am, 10.30 am, 12 noon . confessions after 10 am mass on saturday and on request baptisms on the 2nd saturday of each month at 2 pm. please contact the parish office contacts parish office 8316016 fr michael o’grady
